What is KYC? Know your customer in banking

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 21, 2026•9 min read

KYC, short for know your customer, is the work a bank or fintech does to find out who each customer is, confirm it, understand why they want the account and keep that picture current for as long as the relationship lasts. In the US, KYC covers a set of Bank Secrecy Act requirements. The main ones are the customer identification program at 31 CFR 1020.220, the beneficial ownership rule at 31 CFR 1010.230 and the ongoing due diligence element of the AML program rule at 31 CFR 1020.210.

The sections below cover what KYC means in banking, the four elements FinCEN describes, what KYC data a bank collects and keeps, where higher-risk customers get more scrutiny, and how a team runs the work day to day. The rules cited are the bank rules; the beneficial ownership rule points to parallel identification rules for broker-dealers, mutual funds and futures firms. This guide explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What KYC means in banking

A bank needs to know three things about a customer: who they are, who stands behind them if the customer is a business, and what the account is for. The last one matters because suspicious activity monitoring compares what a customer does with what the bank expected. The FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual calls risk-based due diligence "the cornerstone of a strong BSA/AML compliance program" and says its objective is to let the bank "understand the nature and purpose of customer relationships".

The words vary by firm. Some say know your client, and many say KYC AML to describe the identity work together with the anti-money laundering program it sits in. The US bank rules use "customer", and the CIP rule applies to a person who opens a new account. The FFIEC manual notes that a customer does not include someone who never receives banking services, such as a person whose loan application is denied.

KYC also has an international baseline. Recommendation 10 of the FATF Recommendations says financial institutions should be "prohibited from keeping anonymous accounts or accounts in obviously fictitious names" and sets out the due diligence measures it expects countries to require of them.

The four elements of KYC

When FinCEN finalized its customer due diligence rule in May 2016, it wrote that "there are four core elements of customer due diligence (CDD)" and listed them in the Federal Register notice:

  1. Customer identification and verification.
  2. Beneficial ownership identification and verification.
  3. Understanding the nature and purpose of customer relationships to develop a customer risk profile.
  4. Ongoing monitoring for reporting suspicious transactions and, on a risk basis, maintaining and updating customer information.

The first was already required, the rule added the second, and it wrote the third and fourth into the AML program rules as what FinCEN calls a "fifth pillar". FATF's Recommendation 10 sets out four parallel measures: identify and verify the customer, identify the beneficial owner, understand the purpose and intended nature of the relationship, and conduct ongoing due diligence. Institutions set the extent of each with a risk-based approach.

Identifying and verifying the customer

The CIP rule requires procedures that "enable the bank to form a reasonable belief that it knows the true identity of each customer." Before opening an account, the bank obtains at least a name, a date of birth for an individual, an address and an identification number, which for a US person is a taxpayer identification number. It then verifies identity within a reasonable time after the account opens. It can use documents, such as an unexpired driver's license or passport, non-documentary methods, such as comparing what the customer gave with a consumer reporting agency or public database, or both. Our guide to KYC verification covers those methods and what to do when a check fails. Our guide to what KYC software needs to do goes through each CIP requirement in a table.

Identifying the owners of a business customer

For a legal entity customer, the bank identifies each individual who owns 25 percent or more of the equity interests and one individual with "significant responsibility to control, manage, or direct" the company, such as a chief executive or treasurer. It verifies each one's identity with risk-based procedures that contain at least the elements the CIP rule requires for individual customers. The bank may rely on what the customer tells it about its owners if it has no knowledge of facts that would reasonably call that information into question. Business onboarding is covered on our KYB automation page.

Understanding the relationship

FinCEN's 2016 notice describes the customer risk profile as information gathered at account opening "used to develop a baseline against which customer activity is assessed for suspicious activity reporting." It adds that the profile may, but need not, include risk ratings. The FFIEC manual says there are "no required risk profile categories", and that for lower-risk customers the type of customer, account or product can be enough to show what the relationship is for.

Ongoing monitoring

Under 31 CFR 1020.210(a)(2)(v), a bank's AML program must include ongoing monitoring "to identify and report suspicious transactions and, on a risk basis, to maintain and update customer information", including information about the beneficial owners of legal entity customers. The FFIEC manual says this element "does not impose a categorical requirement" to update customer information on a continuous or periodic basis, and that a bank may set its own risk-based rules for when to update. For an operations team that usually means re-screening, event-driven reviews and a periodic KYC review cycle set by risk.

What KYC data a bank collects and keeps

KYC information falls into a few groups. The table shows what each one holds and where the expectation comes from.

KYC dataWhat it includesSource
Identifying informationName, date of birth for an individual, address, and an identification number (TIN for a US person; for a non-US person a TIN, passport number and country of issuance, or similar)1020.220(a)(2)(i)
Verification recordType of document relied on, its number, place of issuance and dates; the non-documentary methods used and their results; how any substantive discrepancy was resolved1020.220(a)(3)(i)
Ownership and controlEach 25 percent owner and one control person of a legal entity customer, with the certification or equivalent information1010.230(b) and (d)
Customer risk profileNature and purpose of the relationship, and for higher-risk customers more detail, such as source of funds and wealth, occupation or type of business, and expected transaction volumes1020.210(a)(2)(v) and the FFIEC manual
List check resultWhether the customer appears on a list of known or suspected terrorists that Treasury designates for CIP purposes. The FFIEC manual notes that, as of its publication, no such list has been designated1020.220(a)(4)

The CIP rule sets retention. Identifying information is kept for five years after the account closes. The document descriptions, verification methods and discrepancy resolutions are kept for five years after the record is made. Checks against OFAC lists are a separate obligation, covered in our guide to reviewing a sanctions screening hit.

When KYC goes further for higher-risk customers

The FFIEC manual says due diligence procedures "should define both when and what additional customer information will be collected" based on the customer risk profile, and calls this enhanced due diligence. Information from higher-risk customers should be reviewed more closely at account opening and more often afterwards. The manual also says a bank should decide when, on the basis of risk, to run reviews such as negative media searches.

Two account types have their own rules. For correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, 31 CFR 1010.610 requires a due diligence program that assesses each account's money laundering risk and includes periodic review of account activity. For private banking accounts, 31 CFR 1010.620 requires reasonable steps to identify all nominal and beneficial owners and to find out whether any of them is a senior foreign political figure. The bank must also establish the source of funds and the purpose and expected use of the account.

How a bank or fintech team runs KYC

  1. Write the procedure. Set out, per customer type and channel, what to collect, which verification method applies, what counts as a substantive discrepancy and who can approve an exception.
  2. Give notice and collect. Show the customer notice before the account opens, then capture the identifying information. For a business, collect the owner and control person details with the certification or equivalent information.
  3. Verify. Run documentary checks, non-documentary checks or both, and route anything that fails to a reviewer, who applies the procedure on whether the account opens, stays restricted or closes.
  4. Screen. Check the customer and, for a business, each owner against the lists your program uses, and send possible matches to a named reviewer.
  5. Build the risk profile. Record the purpose of the account and expected activity, and assign the profile or rating your program uses.
  6. Decide and record. Approve, decline or approve with conditions, and record the evidence, the reviewer and how any discrepancy was resolved. If identity cannot be verified, follow the procedure: do not open, limit use while verification continues, close, or refer for suspicious activity review.
  7. Keep it current. Re-screen when lists change, review files on the schedule the risk profile sets, and refresh information when something about the customer changes.

Steps 2 to 6 are the KYC onboarding review, and step 7 is the periodic review. Verkflo's KYC automation runs a team's written KYC procedure as a versioned AI agent workflow that pulls applicant data from Sumsub, screens in ComplyAdvantage and pauses for a reviewer where the procedure says so.

What changed in 2026

On February 13, 2026, FinCEN issued order FIN-2026-R001. It lets covered financial institutions identify and verify a legal entity customer's beneficial owners when the customer first opens an account, instead of at every new account. After that, they repeat the work when facts call the information into question or when their ongoing due diligence calls for it. In that last case they may rely on information already held if the customer confirms, verbally or in writing, that it is up to date and accurate, and they must keep a record of that confirmation.

On November 17, 2026, FinCEN issued a proposed rule to strengthen customer due diligence requirements, as part of Treasury's implementation of Executive Order 14406. It is a proposal, so the current rule text still applies.

Common questions

Is KYC a legal requirement for banks?

Yes. US banks must have a written customer identification program, procedures to identify and verify beneficial owners of legal entity customers, and risk-based procedures for ongoing due diligence in their AML program.

Is KYC the same as AML?

No. KYC is one part of an AML program. The bank AML program rule also requires internal controls, independent testing, a designated compliance person and training, alongside the ongoing due diligence element.

Does a bank need the same KYC information from every customer?

No. Beyond the CIP minimums and the ownership information the rule requires at the 25 percent threshold regardless of risk, the FFIEC manual says the level and type of customer information should match the customer risk profile, with more for higher-risk customers.

How long are KYC records kept?

Under the CIP rule, identifying information is kept for five years after the account closes (for credit card accounts, after it closes or becomes dormant), and verification records for five years after they are made.
